newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine to increase 1997 budget deficit - president.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine to increase 1997 budget deficit - president.

text.p: Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma said on Tuesday that this year's budget deficit would rise to six percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from four percent forecast in the first budget draft released last September.

"The deficit in the proposed 1997 budget has been increased to six percent, from four percent forecast in the very first budget proposal," Kuchma told a meeting attended by Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko and industrial leaders.

Parliamentary speaker Olexander Moroz told the same meeting that parliament would only start reviewing the latest draft of this year's budget once it had passed much-delayed tax reforms -- and this could be as late as March.
The constitution says the budget must be approved by January 1 and international lending bodies link aid to the speedy passage of spending plans through parliament.

The deficit had last been forecast at 5.5 percent of GDP, or four percent by Western calculations, in a December draft which received International Monetary Fund (IMF) approval and was expected to pave the way for a $2.5-3 billion loan.
Kuchma did not say how he expected the IMF to react to the predicted increase.
He blamed the increase on deficits from the past two years, which he said official figures underestimated.
"For two years the deficit was disguised and totalled 10 billion hryvnia, taking a large bite out of our revenues. This has caused all of our problems," Kuchma said.
He said GDP fell 10.1 percent in 1996, although government forecasts last year predicted a drop of 7.0 percent.
The 1997 budget draft envisages Ukraine's first economic growth, of 1.7 percent, since it won independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

Ukraine must also pay a wage backlog to doctors, teachers, government workers, students and pensioners which has grown to 3.9 billion hryvnias ($2.1 billion) this month from about $1.5 billion in mid-1996.
Kuchma said the government planned to cut spending, increase treasury bill sales and try to attract more foreign credits to cover the deficit.

"One more option is to print money. But we know what that leads to and we will never agree to it," Kuchma said, referring to previous years when the country printed money and sent inflation skyrocketing.
